## Exposure notes (written by people)

Kept outside the generated section on purpose: these are judgements, not
readings, and they stay until the finding they describe leaves the audit.

- `decode-uri-component` via `expo-router > query-string` (moderate,
  GHSA-vcc3-ghjq-m6fr) was recorded on September 5, 2026 and retired on October
  29, 2026 by the Expo SDK 58 upgrade. `expo-router` 58.0.28 no longer depends
  on `query-string`, so neither package is in the lockfile and the audit no
  longer lists them; a search of the exported iOS, Android and web bundles finds
  neither. While it stood, a malformed percent-encoded link could slow query
  parsing in the app's own process (a nuisance-grade denial of service, no data
  exposed). It was never forced with an npm `overrides` entry: the 0.5.x
  release is ESM-only and `query-string` 7.1.3 loads it with `require()`, which
  would very likely have broken link routing. The deep-link control below stays,
  because the same three routes still read link parameters.
- `zod` (GHSA-mrhx-c7xc-m3w5, high; accepted by Andrew on October 29, 2026,
  review by April 27, 2027, in `audit-accepted.json`): validating an oversized
  constrained collection can exhaust memory. The copy that remains vulnerable
  is 3.25.76, pinned inside `@expo/cli` (the Expo command-line tool). The other
  copy, which came in through ESLint's react-hooks plugin, is 4.6.7 since
  October 29 and is fixed. The remaining copy reads this repository's own
  configuration, not user input, and no app source imports it. The only fixed
  release is 4.6.6 or newer, which `@expo/cli` cannot take; npm's only offer is
  a downgrade to Expo 51, which the prohibition below rules out. Build tooling
  only, not expected in the Android or iOS bundle. Confirmed on October 29,
  2026 against the SDK 58 build: `npx expo export --platform all` output, searched
  for "zod" and "node-forge" in the iOS (Hermes) and Android bundles and the web
  scripts, shows neither. Repeat that search at each release.
- `deepmerge` (GHSA-gcqx-w48m-w2h4, low): `mergeObject()` allows prototype
  poisoning of returned objects. It arrives through `@expo/config` and Jest,
  merging configuration this repository writes. No fixed release exists. Not
  waived by the accept list (low severity needs none); recorded here so it is
  not rediscovered as new.
- `braces` (GHSA-vfj7-8cjw-p6xm) was accepted on October 19, 2026 and withdrawn
  by GitHub on October 23, 2026, so its acceptance was removed on October 29.
- `node-forge` (GHSA-86w9-cpqp-85rv) was accepted on October 19, 2026 because
  no fix existed. Version 1.4.1 published a fix on October 27; the non-forced
  `npm audit fix` took the lockfile to 1.4.2 on October 29, the advisory left
  the audit, and its acceptance was removed. For the record, it reached the
  project only through the `expo-updates` key-generation CLI and `@expo/cli`
  iOS signing-certificate parsing; on the phone, update signatures are verified
  in native code and `scripts/publish-update.mjs` signs with `node:crypto`.
- The high rows in the generated table other than `zod` are dependents (`expo`,
  `@expo/cli`) that npm marks vulnerable because they contain it.
- The October 12 critical, `shell-quote` (GHSA-pqg4-j6r4-53mv, via
  `react-native > react-devtools-core`), was cleared by the October 19 weekly
  run's non-forced `npm audit fix`.
- The August 16 findings (`image-size@1.2.1`, `uuid@7.0.3`) left the
  dependency graph by September 5; `image-size` is gone and `uuid` resolves
  to 11.1.1.
- `@grpc/grpc-js` (GHSA-m9gg-hp2v-232j and GHSA-f596-whhp-79r4, both high)
  arrived on October 29, 2026 with Firebase Analytics: `@react-native-firebase/app`
  depends on Google's `firebase` web SDK, whose Firestore package pins
  `@grpc/grpc-js` ~1.9. Both advisories concern gRPC servers, and the phone apps
  run Firebase's native iOS and Android libraries, not that web SDK, so neither
  was reachable. They were still removed rather than accepted: an npm
  `overrides` entry pins `@grpc/grpc-js` to 1.13.7, the first fixed release.
  The only code that loads it is Firestore's Node.js path, which nothing in the
  app imports.

## Why `npm audit fix --force` is prohibited

The forced path proposes semver-major moves (in September 2026, a downgrade of
`expo-router` to 5.1.11) that do not match the SDK 58 project and would replace
the verified platform foundation with an unsupported dependency combination.
The weekly job runs the non-forced `npm audit fix` only, and keeps its result
only when the mobile tests, typecheck and expo-doctor still pass.

Do not run `npm audit fix --force`.

## Required controls

- Keep Expo and React Native on versions accepted by `npx expo install --check` and `npx expo-doctor`.
- Do not feed untrusted or user-supplied images into the local Metro/build asset pipeline.
- Use only reviewed repository assets during development and CI.
- Re-run the full npm audit at each Expo patch update and before every beta/release build.
- Keep link handling to the parameters read today (`alerts`, `help` and the shared-scenario parameters on `estimate`); any new deep-link parameter re-opens this triage.
- Reassess immediately if the app later adds image import, document upload, or any server-side bundling of user content.
- Block release for any critical advisory or any advisory shown to be reachable in shipped runtime behavior.
- Keep app analytics to `src/lib/usageStats.ts`, with its fixed lists of screens and events, and keep advertising identifiers off in `firebase.json` and `app.json`; `scripts/lib/privacy-config.test.ts` at the repository root enforces both. Any new analytics event or parameter, or any other analytics or advertising library, re-opens the privacy policy and both store privacy forms.
- `firebase/GoogleService-Info.plist` and `firebase/google-services.json` are committed on purpose: they hold the app's public Firebase identifiers and a client API key that Google designs to ship inside every copy of the app, not a secret. Never commit a Firebase service-account key (a JSON file with a `private_key`).

This is a dated triage record derived from the September 1 lockfile, not a
permanent waiver. The dependency state must be re-derived whenever that
lockfile changes, and within 14 days of any release check.

## Standing policy, and how this record stays current

`scripts/audit-triage.mjs --auto` runs every Monday from `mobile-audit.yml`
with nobody watching. It tries the non-forced `npm audit fix` and keeps it
only if the app still checks out; re-runs the audit; rewrites the generated
section above; and stamps the fingerprint and date. Its verdict follows one
rule:

- **No high or critical advisory:** accepted and committed. Moderate and low
  findings with no compatible fix are recorded, not waived; the controls above
  name what reopens them.
- **High advisories a person has already reviewed:** accepted the same way,
  and an open escalation issue is closed. A finding counts as reviewed only
  when every high or critical advisory it traces to is listed in
  `audit-accepted.json` with a
  reason, at the severity npm reports today, before its review date (at most
  six months after acceptance). A critical advisory can never be listed.
- **Any other high or critical advisory:** the record is still written, but
  the run fails and opens a GitHub issue. A person assesses reachability in
  the exposure notes; `check:release` blocks a release while the advisory
  stands. If it is not reachable in shipped runtime behavior and has no fix,
  accepting it means adding an exposure note here and an entry to
  `audit-accepted.json` in the same pull request.

An acceptance ends on its own: a new advisory on the same packages, a severity
raised to critical, or a review date that passes all escalate again.

The release check enforces the 14-day rule, the block on unreviewed high or
critical advisories, and lapsed acceptances when `RELEASE_CHECK=1`; on ordinary
pushes it only warns.
